text:
It Isn’t That You’re Wrong; It’s That You Are Insufferable

     This is the second time inside of a 3-month timeframe that I have felt compelled to tell the diehard pro-gen AI Bros and Hoes to tone it the fuck down. Since they broadly don’t seem capable of civility in any sense of the word, I’ll turn to an approach that they may understand a bit better- put a fucking sock in it.
     The majority of you have become just as insufferable, if not more so, than the whining, whinging, hardcore anti-AI crowd who you so love to clown upon, the digital equivalent of little Prince/King Jauffre from Game of Thrones, and I’d kind of like to see some of you choke to death like he did, eyes goggling out of your heads as your lungs fill with your own liquified tongues and throats. 
     “Whoa, kind of harsh, Josh,” I imagine some might say. Well, tough shit, I would reply. These dickbags like to claim they don’t care anymore what their opposition says, so why offer them decency or softened language, when it doesn’t mean a goddamned thing to them? They’re so ‘above it all’, so fuck the niceties. 
     I’ve tried explaining that I understand that many of them have been under absolutely vicious hostility and pressure from unhinged anti-AI absolutists, and that slightly more empathetic approach got me where, exactly? Aiming for nuance or subtlety gets you nowhere with this crowd, especially when you’re a relative non-entity like I am, so using the megaphone of vitriol starts to look like the only resort left to me. In that vein:
     Fuck Leaflit. Fuck Ember Paradox. To hell with every one of these “OnLy ReSuLtS mAtTeR”, soulless, spiritless, careless GDP-first, Line Go Up, productivity worshipping, inhuman heretics who have decided that only their perspectives are worthy of getting a hearing and holding the floor. Most of them seem to have all of the technical skill in the world, and bully for them, but they also seem to have zero ability to appreciate history or a sense of shared humanity.
     They are lovely little worker drones who will happily declare entire swatches of their fellow humans ‘obsolete’ and whistle Dixie past the graveyard as they skip away from the wreckage left in their wakes. “Get with the times,” they bark. “No one cares how long it took you to acquire these skills, they want results, now!”
     Human beings and their lives beyond their labor value to the market or employers are not line items on a spreadsheet, you feckless cunts! Is it really any wonder that most of these people are uncoupled and childless? Who would want to conceive and raise a kid with such mechanistic freaks of nature? This goes double for the blue-haired slime girl, since she seems to adore telling everyone else that they need to have kids, and she doesn’t seem capable of maintaining a close interpersonal relationship beyond the one she has with her mother. Yes, that’s a personal dig, at this point, she fucking deserves it; you want to demand other people do Thing X so loudly, then lead by example, retard.
     One Carrington Event, and most of these people will become worthless noise holes in faces that deserve a middle finger, a kick in the teeth, and the cold comfort of their own miserable, lonesome company. I almost pray for it at some points when reading/listening to these people.
     “Wagon builders and buggy makers Reeee’d about the automobile too, suck it up, history has no place for losers,” they quip with enough snark to fuel John Oliver for the next decade. Hey, fuck stick, did you know that Henry Ford hired close to 400k cabinet makers, buggy makers, wagoneers and other woodworkers to learn and work in his early shops? The first of his assembly plants was set up in a former woodshop as homage to the roots of transportation! He and his early competitors established ‘trade homes’, communal bunkhouses for displaced artisans to live while they learned assembly work and transitioned to the new labor environment.
     These heavy-handed pro-Gen AI dickheads are way more ‘adapt or die’ than those trailblazers they always seem to love comparing themselves and their efforts to. The whole ‘Automotive Analogy’ falls flat on its ass with even a modicum of examination, so they can fuck off with that.
      Another one they love to trot out and lean into is photography. They’ll point out that the arrival of photography didn’t eliminate visual artists, and they are absolutely correct there. Thank God for people still wanting art that isn’t just documentation of our tangible world. Additionally, a quick question: who did early photographers turn to for analysis and critique of their captured images? Oh, right: artists. Who were the first folks to get instruction and really master the use of the tools of photography in the main? Oh, right: artists. 
     There is always going to be hesitation and skepticism when a new toolset or technology is introduced, a desire to ask for restraint when an altogether foreign or alien way of doing things is presented for consideration. Questions of cost, of by-products, of side effects are natural, human inquiries to pose. Defending one’s known methodology and way of life is a very human impulse. 
     Every time a new technique or technology has been introduced, historically, the creators and early adopters of them have reached out a hand in invitation. With the Gen-AI boosters, there is no extended hand, but rather, middle fingers, insults and invective so laced with nuclear hate and smug superiority that folks drawing near should have Geiger Counters handy.
     It’s generally not advised to engage with those folks in anger, because they find your upset amusing, like most terminally online tech-folk and/or trolls. Certainly I shouldn’t probably be so overtly hostile; it isn’t my work or Art these people are so intent on rendering meaningless right now. They don’t have to; they already cheered that on when ChatGPT and Grok started putting together prompt texts to shunt human efforts aside. 
     They don’t care about you, or me, or any other traditional Artist who has reservations about these supposed technological marvels. Most of them treat life as a game, and their only interest is in winning. But life is not a game; there is no leaderboard, no high score that gets recorded forever. Life is a myriad of stories, an infinitely expanding library of tales written by doing the living itself.
     Well, something like that, anyway. Probably a bad analogy on my part here. Does it matter, though? None of the people this is aimed at are going to read or hear this anyway; they are much-beloved online figures, and I’m an irrelevant anachronism in many ways, hand-writing the draft of this script in a pocket notebook purchased at the local Dollar Tree, scribbling during my breaks at work at my normie job.
     In short, exactly the sort of person whose view counts or livestream donations they want, but whose perspectives and opinions don’t mean shit to them.
     Fuck them.
     I had much nastier things to say to a couple of them, but what’s the point? This wasn’t made with their precious AI, so they wouldn’t notice anyhow.

How the LDS System Survives Every Hit

Watch the move. It is an old one. A salesman holds up the signed warranty, reads it out loud, then after the engine fails says those printed words were only a starting point and the company now has a new policy.

Joseph Smith Jr. and the institution that followed him perfected a modern version of the same tactic. Make a hard claim. Meet the evidence. Change the claim. Keep the authority. Then treat disbelief as a spiritual defect.

Quoting a verse often fails because the method was designed so the living LDS prophet cannot be wrong. The pattern repeats with almost liturgical regularity.

Assert a hard claim. Joseph Smith translated the Book of Abraham from Egyptian papyri he purchased in 1835 and presented the characters as Abraham’s own record. Two personages appeared in the grove in 1820, the Father introducing the Son. There was no polygamy in Nauvoo; Joseph had only one wife. The eighth Article of Faith states: “We believe the Bible to be the word of God as far as it is translated correctly; we also believe the Book of Mormon to be the word of God.” That clause functions as a standing LDS reservation of interpretive power.

Meet contrary evidence. The surviving papyri, examined by Egyptologists after their rediscovery in 1967, are standard late-period funerary texts, not an Abrahamic narrative. Joseph also published Facsimile 1 as a drawing of Abraham on an altar. Egyptologists identify the same vignette as a funerary scene for a priest named Hor, not Abraham. Joseph’s earliest First Vision account, written in his own hand in 1832, speaks of “the Lord” who forgave his sins. It does not describe two distinct personages with the Father introducing the Son, a scene that appears in the later, canonized 1838 version. For decades members were taught the one 1838 story as if it were the only record.

Journals, affidavits, and the 1843 revelation now printed as Doctrine and Covenants 132 show Joseph practicing and authorizing plural marriage while public statements and Times and Seasons articles issued carefully worded denials of “polygamy” and “spiritual wifery.” The Kinderhook plates, a nineteenth-century hoax, produced a reported partial reading linking the find to Ham and Pharaoh. That reading tracks Joseph’s own Egyptian Alphabet rather than any ancient text.

Greek and Hebrew Bible manuscripts do not teach Smith’s later restoration doctrines of a plurality of formed gods or temple exaltation.

The same collision sits inside his restoration scripture. Jacob 2:24, 27 says David and Solomon’s many wives and concubines were “abominable” and commands, “there shall not any man among you have save it be one wife; and concubines he shall have none.” Jacob 2:30 leaves only a narrow exception: God may “command” otherwise to raise up seed. Doctrine and Covenants 132 later commands plural marriage and reverses the judgment on the same kings. D&C 132:1, 34, 38 say Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, David, and Solomon were given many wives and were justified, except David in the case of Uriah. The earlier text is not allowed to judge the later revelation.

Change the claim, keep the authority. The papyri become a “catalyst,” not a translation in the ordinary sense. Joseph’s study of them is said to have prompted a revelation about Abraham even if the characters themselves say something else. The published facsimile is left standing as scripture while its Egyptian meaning is set aside. The 1832 vision is assigned a different audience, more personal, less institutional. Joseph “only meant” civil or unauthorized marriage when he denied polygamy; celestial plural marriage is treated as another category. The Bible remains true “as far as it is translated correctly,” a phrase that lets Smith and later LDS prophets decide which verses survive intact. The Church’s Gospel Topics essays now concede the hard documents, offer new theories, and leave the prophet’s office untouched.

The LDS prophet’s office is never surrendered. Only the content of the original assertion is quietly retired.

Make disbelief a spiritual defect. If the new explanation does not satisfy you, you lack a testimony. You were never truly converted. You have allowed “the philosophies of men” to spoil you. The living LDS oracle remains the standard. The biblical text is allowed to lose.

The LDS Church can always produce a reply. It cannot produce the original Egyptian Abraham, a First Vision account from 1832 that already contains the later Godhead scene, a Kinderhook text that is ancient, or a King James Bible that teaches a plurality of formed gods and a gospel of temple exaltation. Those things are not missing because critics hid them. They are missing because they were never there.

The Bible already named this method:
“Howbeit in vain do they worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men.” (Mark 7:7)

“Making the word of God of none effect through your tradition.” (Mark 7:13)

“Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men.” (Colossians 2:8)

Jesus’ move is the opposite of Smith’s restoration hierarchy. Biblical scripture judges tradition. Isaiah 8:20 says, “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.” The Bereans in Acts 17:11 tested even apostolic preaching by the scriptures daily. Galatians 1:8 binds an apostle, and even an angel, to the gospel already delivered. Living LDS authority does not get to empty a verse and keep the verse’s prestige.

The KJV biblical witness confronting the LDS Church is not only a contest over grammar. It is a contest over who is allowed to be wrong.

When a Bible verse and an LDS prophet contradict, which one is allowed to be wrong?

Prime example:
Isaiah 43:10 in the KJV: “Ye are my witnesses, saith the LORD, and my servant whom I have chosen: that ye may know and believe me, and understand that I am he: before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me.”

Set that against Joseph Smith’s King Follett teaching and later restoration doctrine that God was once a man, that other gods were formed, and that faithful men may themselves become gods. The Bible verse is not permitted to stand as written. Joseph Smith’s later word is.

“It’s almost as if God told him to make this statue.”

EXACTLY. That is the point.

If making a religious image were intrinsically idolatrous, then God could not have commanded Moses to make the bronze serpent (Numbers 21:8–9), commanded the Israelites to make TWO GOLDEN CHERUBIM over the Ark (Exodus 25:18–22), or permitted the Temple to be filled with carved cherubim, palm trees, flowers, lions and oxen (1 Kings 6:23–35; 7:25–36).

So the biblical commandment obviously does NOT mean, “Never make a religious image.” It means: do not make an image into a GOD and worship it as such.

And your “billions of idols to Mary and other dead people” line is just begging the question. Calling something an “idol” does not magically make it one. An idol is an object worshipped as a deity. Catholics do not believe Mary is God. Catholics do not believe the saints are gods. Catholics do not offer them the adoration owed to the Trinity.

And no, Scripture does not need a verse saying, “Thou shalt manufacture Catholic statues.” Scripture also never commands Christians to print billions of Bibles, build church steeples, use microphones, make Nativity scenes, or put crosses on church buildings. “Show me the verse commanding this exact practice” is not an argument that the practice is forbidden.

Better still, your own Bible depicts heavenly saints consciously presenting the prayers of the faithful before God: Revelation 5:8 speaks of the elders holding bowls of incense, “which are the prayers of the saints,” and Revelation 8:3–4 depicts heavenly presentation of prayers before God.

So please decide what your argument actually is.

If your argument is “all sacred images are idols,” Exodus 25 destroys it.

If your argument is “all bowing before an image is worship,” Joshua 7:6 gives you Joshua falling face-down before the Ark.

If your argument is “the saints are simply dead and cut off from us,” Jesus says God “is not God of the dead, but of the living” (Luke 20:38).

And if your argument has now retreated to “God never specifically commanded Catholics to make billions of statues,” then you have abandoned your original claim. Something does not become idolatry merely because Scripture does not contain a numerical production order for it.

The Bible condemns IDOLATRY. Catholics condemn idolatry too.

What the Bible does not teach is your invented equation:

IMAGE = IDOL
HONOR = WORSHIP
SAINT = GOD

Those equations come from you, not Scripture.

You said, “I’ll wait.”

Some people keep worrying that “there is no salt for the porridge.”

Some others keep worrying that “there is no sugar for the coffee.”

We belong to the first category.

The temples in big cities receive enormous income. 
Devotees flock to them in large numbers. But shouldn’t at least some people visit the small, remote villages, have darshan at the Perumal and Shiva temples there, and see for themselves how those temples are being maintained?
The people performing kainkaryam (service to the deity) there are human beings too. They have families. Who is there to support them?

In a small villages, one Gurukkal alone may be responsible for at least five or six temples. We should think seriously about this.

Every single day, without fail—whether he is physically strong or unwell, whether it rains or the sun blazes—he struggles to travel from one temple to another on his TVS 50, spending heavily on petrol. 

He opens each temple, lights the lamps, offers a pot of water, removes the old clothes from the deity and adorns the deity with fresh garments, flowers.
 
He may offer just four nandiyavattai flowers that he has personally brought with him. 

He then shows the Mahānaivedyam, carried in a tin-coated brass container, to all the sanctums, closes the temple again, and proceeds to the next temple.

Who is there to look after such a person?

In city temples, there are security guards and other staff. 

But in remote villages, the Gurukkal has to take care of everything.

This is the reality.

I have said this many times before.
Please, for the sake of the remote villages, support those priests who perform kainkaryam there and their families. 

Give generously and often.

Your future generations will prosper greatly.
In city temples, a Gurukkal or priest may receive ₹2,000–₹2,500 in offerings on the plate in a single day, from both pujas together—and sometimes even more.

But for the Sivacharyars and Bhattars in remote villages, it may take one or even two months to receive such an amount in their offering plates.

In many temples, the administration has also deteriorated. The hereditary trustees may have passed away two or three generations ago, and their descendants may not be responsibly managing the temples. 

Temple properties have changed hands over generations, lease payments are pending, and lands that were set aside for the support of the Gurukkals are not being properly measured or managed. Even the small income that should come from those lands often does not reach them.

Hundreds or even thousands of veli of land that once belonged to the deity many years ago have changed hands and been leased to various people. 

Today, recovering those properties itself is a great challenge. In some cases, it is not even clear in whose name the patta is registered.

Therefore, those who perform kainkaryam in such temples have zero assured monthly income.

Now, please think deeply.

If your heart feels that you should help such remote village temples, please do it immediately—without delay.

I can give you their phone numbers and bank details. 

Please help in whatever way you can.
When you feel inspired to do a good deed, do it immediately, before the mind changes.

Even one rupee that you give to a Sivacharyar or an archakar may help pay for medicines, blood-pressure or diabetes tablets, an insulin injection, or an eye operation.

When you extend your support to them, Bhagavan accepts it as service to Him and blesses you with welfare and well-being.

If their families live in comfort and security, we too will live even better.

Siva, Siva, Siva. 🙏

A failed car bomb in Times Square, a name misspelled on a watch list, a brother who flew home from six months in a militant stronghold unnoticed — the pattern holds across every case: the system caught up after the fact, never before it.
Chapter 6 — The Human Intelligence Problem: FBI, CIA, and the Allies (2/2)
Shahzad. Faisal Shahzad, a naturalized U.S. citizen who traveled to the Waziristan region of Pakistan and received explosives training from Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan, financed his operation through an informal hawala money-transfer network that bypassed the formal financial surveillance tripwires established by the USA PATRIOT Act, and left an explosive device in a parked Nissan Pathfinder in Times Square on May 1, 2010. The device failed. Street vendors noticed smoke coming from the vehicle and alerted the NYPD. The New York Joint Terrorism Task Force identified him within roughly forty-eight hours. Despite his name being quickly added to the No-Fly list, Shahzad nonetheless managed to board a flight bound for Dubai at John F. Kennedy International Airport and was apprehended only minutes before the aircraft was cleared for takeoff. There was no pre-attack tip and no confidential human source. The Commission noted that broader domain awareness of Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan-related travel and training might have identified Shahzad before his attempt; it did not. What worked was the post-event Joint Terrorism Task Force machine — NYPD detectives, FBI agents, and federal technical collection operating at high speed. That is a different competence from preventive HUMINT, and the near-miss at JFK undercut any narrative that the post-9/11 watchlisting and border-security dragnet had become foolproof.
The Tsarnaevs. In March 2011 the Russian Federal Security Service warned the FBI about Tamerlan Tsarnaev. The Boston Field Office opened an assessment, interviewed him, checked databases, and closed the matter after finding no nexus to terrorism. The CIA separately nominated him for watchlisting, entering his name on a Customs and Border Protection watch list. When Tsarnaev flew to Russia in January 2012, that entry correctly triggered an alert at JFK; CBP flagged him as a passenger of concern but judged him a low priority against roughly a hundred other names on the list that day and let him board. Sometime that fall, in a records refresh unrelated to any new derogatory reporting, his surname was mistakenly re-entered into the watch list as "Tsarnayev." When he returned to the United States in July 2012 after six months in Dagestan, the misspelled entry did not match his travel documents, no alert fired, and no one — not CBP, not the FBI — flagged his re-entry or followed up. A 2014 House Homeland Security Committee report confirmed the sequence. In April 2013 the brothers detonated pressure-cooker bombs at the Boston Marathon. Mosque contacts and family members later described a radicalization that had been visible in retrospect and unreported in prospect; the Commission specifically noted that information about Tamerlan's outbursts during sermons at the Islamic Society of Boston Cultural Center in Cambridge had not reached the Bureau in a form that changed the assessment. Analysts played a minor role in the 2011 review. No human source in Boston's Chechen or Islamist milieu flagged Tamerlan as he moved from person of interest to operational attacker, and the one technical safeguard that might have caught his return from six months in a militant stronghold failed on a clerical error. The record converges on the same institutional pattern found across the other four cases: a lead arrived from an outside source; the assessment was conducted as a discrete inquiry rather than as the start of domain coverage; the file closed.
Taken together, the five cases do not prove that FBI HUMINT never works; the Commission itself noted other disrupted plots outside the test set. What the five cases do prove is narrower and more useful. Against homegrown or hybrid actors — U.S. persons or residents with some foreign training or inspiration, operating in small groups or alone, communicating online, radicalizing inside institutions the Bureau does not own — the post-2005 HUMINT program did not generate the first alert. Technical collection, foreign liaison, chance witnesses, and failed devices did. The Commission's forward-looking conclusion was that FISA and related authorities remained essential, and that HUMINT needed programmatic guidance, better domain tasking, and a career system that rewarded sources against emerging threats rather than sources who closed existing cases.
That is a different failure mode from 2001. In 2001 the Bureau often did not know what it knew. In 2009-2013 it often knew something and still did not have a human source who could turn "something" into "this person, this week, this target."
IV. CIA VERSUS FBI HUMINT: THE STRUCTURAL SEAM
The legal architecture underneath the five cases is older than any of them. The CIA's National Clandestine Service — renamed the Directorate of Operations in 2015 — collects foreign human intelligence under Title 50 authorities; it may not exercise law-enforcement powers or internal-security functions, a limit rooted directly in the 1947 National Security Act's original charter language. The FBI collects domestic intelligence and runs human sources under Title 18 and Title 28 authorities, the Attorney General's Guidelines, and a national-security mission bolted onto a law-enforcement statute after 2001. Overseas, FBI Legal Attaches work with CIA chiefs of station under a 2005 memorandum of understanding that the 2015 Commission described as leaving the relationship "arguably the strongest it has been in their collective history." Domestically, the seam is harder.
A source who begins as an FBI informant on a U.S.-based threat and then develops foreign ties, or a CIA asset whose reporting touches a person inside the United States, recreates the pre-9/11 problem in miniature. IRTPA's creation of the National Counterterrorism Center was supposed to sit across that seam. Section 1021 of IRTPA gave NCTC the specific authority to "receive, retain, and disseminate" domestic counterterrorism intelligence in furtherance of its mission — the single statutory mechanism that let the Center fuse CIA and NSA foreign reporting with financial, travel, immigration, and local law-enforcement data collected domestically by the FBI and the Department of Homeland Security. The Terrorist Identities Datamart Environment, the resulting repository of derogatory information on known or suspected terrorists, grew by some estimates to more than a million distinct identities by the late 2010s, which created a downstream analytical problem of its own: finding signal inside an overwhelming volume of noise, and continuously refining the criteria for exporting names from TIDE to the FBI's Terrorist Screening Center and its actionable Terrorist Screening Database, including the No-Fly List. NCTC was also, by design and by subsequent legal interpretation, limited in what it could do with purely domestic information and barred from itself becoming an operational service against domestic targets.
The legislative mandate drove a broader cultural shift the community summarized as moving from "need to know" — a Cold War compartmentation principle meant to protect sources and methods — to "need to share." That shift proved easier to legislate than to practice. Agencies remained protective of sources and jurisdictional turf, frequently downgrading or over-redacting reports before pushing them to state and local fusion centers, which left much of the shared product too thin for tactical use; audits repeatedly found that information sharing in the field still ran on personal relationships between individual agents and analysts rather than on institutionalized, scalable processes.
Hoffman, testifying before HPSCI on May 20, 2026, called the domestic-action bar "a dangerous anachronism," arguing that the principal analytic integrator of terrorist threats was legally prevented from acting on the part of the threat that now most often materializes inside the United States. The 2015 Commission had already watched that anachronism operate in the Hasan case, where FBI, DoD, and NCTC sharing was inadequate, and in the Tsarnaev case, where a foreign lead, a CIA watchlist nomination, and an FBI assessment failed to become a single running picture.
The seam is not only legal. It is cultural. CIA case officers are trained to recruit and run sources whose value is measured in reporting, not in prosecutions. FBI handling of confidential human sources is still shaped by the possibility that the source will become a witness, that the relationship will be discoverable, and that the agent's performance will be judged by the case that results. Those are rational incentives. They are not the same incentives. A source who can describe a foreign training camp but cannot testify is a CIA success and an FBI complication. A source who can wear a wire against a U.S. person is an FBI success and, if the person has foreign co-conspirators, a CIA coordination problem. The 2005 memorandum of understanding and the growth of joint task forces reduced the frequency of open conflict. They did not abolish the two different theories of what a human source is for.
Headley sits exactly on the seam. He had been a U.S. law-enforcement informant. He became a Lashkar-e-Taiba operative. His wives' warnings landed in the U.S. government and died there. Mumbai was a foreign mass-casualty attack planned with the help of an American who had once been on the books of a U.S. agency. Denmark was the sequel that the FBI stopped, again not because a source inside Headley's life had come forward, but because another lead finally forced the Bureau to look. The 2015 Commission did not need a new theory of the CIA-FBI divide to explain Headley. It needed only to notice that the divide still described the file.
V. FIVE EYES, MI5, AND MI6
The British comparison is the one American reformers reach for when they want to argue that the FBI's dual mandate is the problem. The United Kingdom splits foreign human intelligence (the Secret Intelligence Service, MI6, also called SIS) from domestic security intelligence (the Security Service, MI5) and signals intelligence (GCHQ) in a way that looks, on an organization chart, like CIA and FBI. The resemblance is misleading in the place that matters. Operating primarily under the Security Service Act of 1989 and the Intelligence Services Act of 1994, MI5 is a security service, not a police force, and holds no executive power of arrest. It does not prosecute. It investigates, advises, and hands executive action to the police — since 2006, primarily to Counter Terrorism Command and the regional Counter Terrorism Units — when a case is to be disrupted in public. Because MI5 cannot itself make an arrest, it depends entirely on seamless collaboration with those police units to execute any disruption, which forces intelligence and law enforcement to collaborate by design rather than by choice. Its culture is built around subjects of interest, investigative priorities, and the management of risk across a known universe of people, not around the assembly of trial-ready cases. That difference is the one British officials and the Intelligence and Security Committee have repeatedly cited when explaining why MI5 can keep more people in a lower-level investigative holding pattern than the FBI can. To bridge MI5, MI6, GCHQ, and law enforcement, the UK established the Joint Terrorism Analysis Centre in 2003, housed at MI5's Thames House headquarters and functioning conceptually much like the American NCTC. British counterterrorism strategy, known as CONTEST, is organized around four strands — Prevent, Pursue, Protect, and Prepare — with MI5's operational focus falling heavily under Pursue.
The July 7, 2005 London bombings tested that model in the same way the five American cases tested the FBI. Two of the bombers, Mohammad Sidique Khan and Shehzad Tanweer, had appeared on the periphery of the 2003-2004 investigation codenamed Operation CREVICE, which successfully thwarted a large ammonium nitrate fertilizer-bomb plot in southeast England. Through physical surveillance and bugged vehicles, MI5 photographed Khan, recorded his voice, and traced his vehicle registration; the agency had, in other words, already crossed paths with two future suicide bombers. Under MI5's prioritization matrix, subjects were categorized as either "Essential" or "Desirable" targets, and because Khan and Tanweer were observed only on the periphery of the main CREVICE plotters rather than at its center, they were classed as lower-tier, and active dedicated surveillance was not placed on them. When the CREVICE network was rolled up, MI5 shifted its finite surveillance teams to other tier-one threats and dropped coverage of Khan entirely. Resource constraints were severe enough that the Intelligence and Security Committee's later reporting suggested MI5 could properly track well under a tenth of its subjects of interest at the time, forcing the service into a constant triage against a threat environment larger than its surveillance capacity. The Intelligence and Security Committee's 2006 report found no negligence sufficient to say the attacks would have been prevented, but it found "intelligence gaps," resource constraints, and decisions that, in hindsight, might have been taken differently. The Committee's 2009 follow-up review, "Could 7/7 Have Been Prevented?," reconstructed the CREVICE link from original operational material and reached a similar institutional conclusion: the bombers had been seen; they had not been prioritized; seeing is not the same as covering. Language skills, coverage of Pakistan travel, and the speed of radicalization were named as structural weaknesses. None of that is alien to the Hasan or Tsarnaev files.
Subsequent British reviews after the 2017 attacks at Westminster, Manchester, and London Bridge repeated the pattern at higher resolution. Several attackers were closed subjects of interest or, in one case, an active one. Internal MI5 and police reviews produced more than a hundred recommendations on data exploitation, sharing with neighborhood policing, and consistent assessment regardless of ideology. Partly in response to those failures, the UK unveiled the Counter Terrorism Operations Centre in 2021, co-locating MI5, MI6, GCHQ, and police elements in a single operational space to work counterterrorism as one team rather than as liaising services. The official position, stated across more than a decade of Intelligence and Security Committee reports, is that a security-service model still misses people, that finite surveillance capacity forces triage, and that triage will sometimes be wrong. The claimed advantage over the FBI is not omniscience. It is that MI5's default question is "should this person remain a subject of interest?" rather than "is there a case?"
Five Eyes information sharing — the UKUSA lineage that now includes the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand — does not dissolve these domestic-model differences. It moves foreign-collected intelligence, signals in particular, across the alliance with a density that has no peacetime precedent. Human intelligence is shared more selectively, because human sources are more perishable and more politically sensitive than intercepts. The Zazi investigation benefited from that architecture: the first indications that put him in motion were not a Denver informant but liaison and technical collection that the alliance is built to carry. The Tsarnaev assessment began with a Russian warning that was not a Five Eyes product at all, a reminder that the alliance is not the world. Where Five Eyes helps the HUMINT problem is mostly indirect. It can tell a service that a U.S. or British person trained abroad. It cannot, by itself, produce a source in a Boston apartment or a Yorkshire mosque.
The honest comparison, then, is not that Britain solved the problem the United States failed to solve. It is that a security-service culture changes the error one makes. The FBI's error in the five cases was closing assessments that a security service might have kept lukewarm. MI5's error on July 7 was keeping two future bombers lukewarm when a different triage might have made them hot. Both errors are the price of finite coverage. Only one of them is compounded by the need to build a prosecutable file.
VI. TWENTY-FIVE YEARS ON: THE 2026 LOOK-BACK
The geopolitical paradigm of the 2020s reshaped the counterterrorism mission that the 2004 architecture had been built around. The U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021 and the resurgence of the Taliban cost the CIA its primary forward-operating bases and HUMINT networks in the region, forcing a return to "over-the-horizon" technical collection — precisely the vulnerability that predated 9/11. Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine and escalating strategic competition with China prompted the National Security Council to reprioritize collection targets away from terrorism. Intelligence resources were simultaneously redirected toward transnational criminal organizations, including Mexican drug cartels newly designated as foreign terrorist organizations, stretching an already thin counterterrorism apparatus further.
On August 31, 2026, at the Flight 93 National Memorial in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, HPSCI released a bipartisan review of the intelligence-related recommendations of the 2004 9/11 Commission. Chairman Rick Crawford and Ranking Member Jim Himes framed the document as a twenty-five-year scorecard. Hoffman testified before the Committee on May 20, 2026, warning that continuous budget cuts to counterterrorism programs, the exodus of experienced personnel to China and Russia desks, and the general demotion of terrorism as a national security priority were recreating the exact conditions of under-resourcing and institutional neglect that had preceded the 2001 attacks. The report's center of gravity was not a new HUMINT doctrine. It was the unfinished business of integration: congressional oversight still split between authorizing and appropriating committees; the Director of National Intelligence still weaker in budget power than the 9/11 Commission had wanted; information sharing still a "work in progress"; agency stovepipes still the default; new threats — great-power competition, cyber operations, unmanned systems, homegrown attackers who leave a thin foreign signature — pressing against an architecture designed to connect al-Qaeda dots. Committee members separately noted that the Office of the Director of National Intelligence itself had grown, in one description offered during the review, "way bigger than we ever expected it to be," suffering from mission creep that experts argued should be reversed in favor of returning the office to its core functions of budget oversight, authorities management, and integration.
On the FBI-CIA seam the 2026 report was continuous with 2015 rather than a break from it. Post-9/11 reforms, it found, had improved coordination "primarily in the counterterrorism space." NCTC had "played a vital role" and had helped prevent large-scale attacks of the 2001 type. The domestic-exception problem remained. Hoffman's "dangerous anachronism" line was entered into the record as the Committee's sharpest formulation of the gap IRTPA never closed: the integrator of terrorist threats is not the operator against the domestic ones, and the operator against the domestic ones is still an agency that thinks like a prosecutor when it is not being told, from the top, to think like a service. The report also revisited the Hasan case specifically, noting that his prior contact with a known terrorist in Yemen had been information "not available to all agencies" at the time — the same information-sharing seam the 2015 Commission had already documented — and separately noted that in the December 2009 Abdulmutallab case, information "was available to all-source analysts at the CIA and NCTC prior to the attempted attack," but "the dots were never connected," a "component failure to connect the dots rather than a lack of information sharing," in President Obama's own framing, already treated at length in this study's chapter on IRTPA.
The Committee's own recommendations ran toward mission-centered task forces, interoperable sharing systems, joint duty, and a reinforced NCTC, not toward a new domestic intelligence agency. That choice, too, was continuous with 2004. The original Commission rejected an American MI5. HPSCI in 2026 did not reverse it.
What the 2026 report did not do is claim that the HUMINT gap identified in 2015 had been closed. It did not revisit Zazi, Headley, Hasan, Shahzad, or the Tsarnaevs as a new test set. It treated the absence of another 9/11-scale foreign-directed mass-casualty attack on the homeland as evidence that the larger reform project had been, in Hoffman's phrase from the same hearing, a "towering achievement" — and then immediately placed that achievement against a threat landscape the 2004 Commission had not been asked to imagine. Homegrown attackers, the report noted, often do not exhibit the foreign-actor indicators the post-9/11 system was built to notice. That sentence is the 2015 five-case chapter written for a different decade.
VII. WHAT THE RECORD ACTUALLY SHOWS
The human-intelligence problem after 9/11 is not that the United States failed to build institutions. It built them: a Directorate of Intelligence, a National Security Branch, Field Intelligence Groups, an expanded Joint Terrorism Task Force system, a National Counterterrorism Center, a Director of National Intelligence, a rewritten set of Attorney General Guidelines, and a CIA clandestine service that no longer operates under the mid-1990s scrub as a formal bar. The problem is that those institutions still optimize for different outputs. The FBI produces cases and, increasingly, disruptions. The CIA produces foreign reporting. NCTC produces integration that stops at the edge of domestic action. MI5, the comparison case, produces coverage of subjects of interest and still misses bombers who were already on camera.
The 2015 Commission's twelve findings, read as a set, said the same thing in bureaucratic language. Progress was real. Leadership turnover diluted it. Analysts were more professional than in 2001 and still not empowered as a class. HUMINT guidance in the field was inconsistent. Legal authorities were indispensable. No new evidence changed the 9/11 Commission's account of responsibility for the attacks themselves. The five-case chapter was the empirical core. Everything around it was the attempt to explain why a functioning HUMINT program did not, in the cases that mattered most to the public, function as warning.
That is the through-line from the Phoenix memo to Fort Hood to Boylston Street to Hoffman's 2026 testimony. The United States got better at sharing what it had already collected. It got better at hunting people once a name existed. It did not get reliably good at placing a human source next to the person who did not yet have a file. Church Committee caution, Deutch-era risk aversion, FBI case culture, the Title 50/Title 18 split, and the finite capacity that forces every service to triage are not four or five separate histories, wrongly compressed into a single "the 1970s reforms broke the CIA" story. They are one history with different letterheads, and getting the Church Committee's actual findings right — a reform of unconstitutional domestic abuses, not a ban on foreign recruitment — matters for understanding what would and would not fix the problem going forward.
The allies do not escape it. They allocate the error differently. Twenty-five years after the attacks, that is the HUMINT problem that remains.

text:
Trump Says Iran War Will End ‘Very Shortly’ After Midterm

@LibertarianInst 

President Donald Trump said Americans should expect the war against Iran to continue through November’s midterm elections, predicting the conflict will end shortly afterward. Meanwhile, the Department of War is preparing to maintain a major US military presence in the Middle East through the end of the year.

“The war will be over very shortly after the election,” the President told the Republican convention in Dallas on Wednesday. Iran is “hanging out for dear life, hoping that we lose so they can deal with dumb, weak Democrats.”

The Department of War plans to maintain at least two aircraft carrier strike groups in the Middle East through the end of the year. Currently, the USS George Washington and George HW Bush are operating in the region. The Washington recently arrived in the Middle East to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln after a record-long deployment.

Officials told The Atlantic that the Navy is now preparing the USS Theodore Roosevelt for a deployment to the region to relieve the Washington. While Trump hopes to end the war after the midterm election, sources told the outlet that some of the President’s aides believe the war will last longer.

According to The Atlantic, Trump believes the US must regain control of the Strait of Hormuz before he can declare victory. Iran has restricted traffic through the waterway, imposed approved shipping lanes and required some vessels to pay a “service fee.” The US has attempted to break Tehran’s control by escorting tankers through the Strait.

While US officials have claimed that the amount of oil exiting the Strait is close to prewar levels, monitoring agencies say only a small fraction is getting out of the Persian Gulf.

Iran’s control over the Strait of Hormuz has led to a spike in global energy prices. On Wednesday, Brent crude closed at over $100 per barrel. The increase in the price of oil has hit Americans hard at the pump. The average price of a gallon of regular gasoline is now over $4, and diesel is at record highs.

Trump predicted that gas prices will quickly fall after the war ends and eventually settle below $2 per gallon.

During his speech to the Republican convention, Trump argued he had no choice but to attack Iran because Tehran was on the brink of obtaining nuclear weapons. “We have no choice, right?” He added, “Can Iran have a nuclear weapon? Absolutely not. Well, then I’m right. Then I win.”

However, the President has not presented evidence that Iran is working on a nuclear weapon. The international nuclear watchdog, the IAEA, and the US intelligence community have both assessed that Iran was not working on a nuclear weapon before the US and Israel attacked.

Additionally, before the war, Tehran offered significant restrictions on its nuclear program in exchange for US sanctions relief.

The Psi Corps was an Earth Alliance organization, ostensibly established to help human telepaths learn how to control and use their abilities for the betterment of themselves and Humanity at large.

Culture of The Corps
📷Psi Corps Badge
Psi Corps culture naturally grew out what had already been established by the Metasensory Regulation Authority, some of which came straight from The Kith. The phrase perhaps most synonymous with the Corps, "The Corps is Mother, The Corps is Father" came from MRA agent Desa Alexander, who along with her fellow Kith made a definite impression on Corps culture. She was frequent to remind her charges while training and tracking down blips that "The kith is mother. The kith is father." Another tradition that began with Alexander and one followed by many was the passing of family names within the Corps along the female line, rather than the male. Referred to as "Mitochondrial descent", the reason behind it was because the marker for the telepath gene was encoded within a teep's mitochondrial DNA. As such, Lyta Alexander could trace her linage back six generations to Desa herself, while Talia Winters inherited her name from former blip and resistance member Jenny Winters.[1] The practice was not totally pervasive however, and by the 2250s it had become something only really associated with the older families of the Corps.[2]
Children raised by the Corps were quickly and thoroughly indoctrinated. Raised mostly in Teeptown, they were kept in small groups or cadres where they were instilled with a sense of belonging and loyalty to a larger body, discouraging individual thinking and other solitary activities. Latents, children who had tested positive as teeps but had yet to manifest their psi abilities were kept in a separate dorm (sometimes called "the basement"), often shunned and rarely mixing with the others, however, once their talents manifested they would quickly be integrated into a proper cadre. Young teeps were taught that they were rare, special, and better than mundanes, and that two teeps should never be seen fighting in front of a normal.[2]
It is the position of the Psi Corps that telepathic humans who do not learn how to control their abilities are mostly unstable or become insane, therefore they need guidance. In addition to that, unregistered telepaths can do severe damage to society by using their abilities for criminal reasons.
Under Earth Alliance law, all human telepaths have to be registered with the Psi Corps. After that, they have three choices: Join the Psi Corps, lifetime imprisonment, or take drugs called sleepers to suppress their abilities. Most choose to work for Psi Corps, because one common side effect of the sleepers is severe depression, sometimes so severe that it often ends in the patient's suicide.[3] Unstable telepaths - such as schizophrenic ones - are locked away for "the good of everyone".[4]
Always an insular organization, Psi Corps would always try to deal with incidents (or "family matters") concerning telepaths internally and tried to avoid interference by mundanes. Believing that as long as normals were kept convinced "nothing goes wrong behind these walls", they would be left alone.[4]
I pledge my body, heart, soul and mind to the service of the Earth Alliance, and the people who dwell on her myriad spheres.
I promise to keep the laws, to keep the faith, to keep my eyes on the truth.
I pledge to serve my comrades, my cadre, and The Corps.
The Corps teaches, guides, and provides. The Corps is mother, the Corps is father.
We are the children of The Corps.
– The Psi Corps pledge.
Propaganda
To strengthen the dedication of telepaths to the Corps, there are a variety of slogans that shall remind the Telepaths, that Psi Corps is their family: -
"The Corps is mother, the Corps is father."
"The Psi Corps is your friend. Trust the Corps."
📷Psi Corps propaganda during an ISN transmission of 36 Hours.
"We’re everywhere. For your convenience."
"Protect the Family."
"Obey."
"Trust the Corps."

"Maternis, Paternis"

"United in thought, revered in memory."

Resources

Psi Corps facilities were spread across the Earth Alliance, from the Corps' headquarters in Earthdome to a secret intelligence center in Syria Planum on Mars.

The facilities at Earthdome featured hospitals, offices, and the Psi Corps Academy where young teeps and teeks were trained to make the best of their talents. Located nearby in Geneva was Teeptown, an enclosed community the size of a large village. Built out from the old MRA MetaSensory compound, this was where new members (mostly children) were indoctrinated into the culture and thinking of Psi Corps.

Unknown to many at the time, Psi Corps secretly maintained a series of motherships that remained in hyperspace. Ferrying Psi Cops back and forth on missions, the motherships only exited to normal space when maintenance and repairs were essential and could be done unobserved.
Psi Cops
📷Psi Cop training
Psi Cops is the collective name for officers of the Metasensory Police, or MetaPol and were the police enforcement arm of Psi Corps, usually dealing with cases relating to telepaths, mostly rogues and blips. All Psi Cops are P-12s,[5] the highest (natural) rating within the Psi Scale, but not every P-12 has the ability to become a Psi Cop, because it takes a certain amount of ruthlessness. Psi Cops receive a special training in blocking and scanning so that they are able to resist a deep-scan for at least an hour.[4]
Following the dissolution of the Psi Corps at the end of the Telepath War, the role of the Psi Cops was divided between the new Bureau of Telepath Integration and the new Metasensory Division of the Earth Alliance Bureau of Investigation.
Bloodhound Units

Bloodhound units are specially trained telepaths under the authority of the Psi Cops, used to hunt down fugitives through empathic tracking and scanning of witnesses, informants and suspects.
The origins of the Bloodhound Units go back to the days of the Metasensory Regulation Authority and a group of agents lead by Desa Alexander (also known as "Blood").[1]

Up until President Morgan Clark's increased dependence on the Psi Corps for civil intelligence gathering and black ops, the Bloodhounds were kept within the Corps, tracking blips and occasionally protecting their own.
One such incident occurred around 2253, when a serial killer murdered a string of commercial telepaths. With the "mundane" authorities seemingly uninterested in catching the perpetrator, the Psi Corps took matters into its own hands without such encumbrances as warrants, permission or due process. Illegally scanning anyone who might have a lead, the Bloodhounds left behind no traces save for lingering memory gaps, missing hours and headaches, eventually finding the killer. Reasoning that turning him over to the proper authorities would require an explanation as to how they found him, the Corps had him sent to an institution on Beta Colony instead, but not before they implanted visions and hallucinations in his mind so terrifying that he would spend the rest of his days and nights screaming at things that only he could see. To prevent him from clawing his own eyes out, he was kept in a straitjacket 24 hours a day.[6]
During the Earth Alliance Civil War, Bloodhound units were assigned to the Earthforce military divisions and bases occupying Mars. Anyone suspected of being a member of the resistance was subjected to a very deep scan. Given the nature of such invasive scans, they were prone to causing heart attacks, seizures, strokes, and even death.[6]

In 2262 the Bloodhound units were dispatched alongside Alfred Bester to hunt down Byron's dissident telepaths.[7][8]
Directors of Psi Corps
A lifelong position, the position of Director of Psi Corps was initially filled by normals who were appointed by the Earth Senate as stipulated in the Psi Corps' original charter. Eventually the position was given over to telepaths.

Terminology

Basement: Informal name given to the dormitory for latent children. These children are kept separate from other telepaths until their abilities manifest, at which point they are integrated into an appropriate Cadre.[2]

Black Omega: Elite Starfury unit attached to Psi Corps.[9]
Blip: a general term used by security officers for fugitives from the law, though it has also become synonymous with rogue telepaths.[9][10] "Type A" Blips are considered to be merely misguided and open to re-education. "Type C" Blips are those who are considered sociopaths or "born criminals", who enjoy abusing their abilities and are much more difficult to re-educate.[2]

Bloop: Referring to the involuntary broadcasting of stray thoughts, either through weak blocks, poor discipline and/or loss of control through panic and emotional distress. Very young or untrained teeps, as well as teeks of any age are particularly notorious for blooping.[2]

Block: Telepathic guard against active scanning or passive sensing. Blocks usually take the form of repeating songs, nursery rhymes, or mathematical calculations.[11][12] With training, mundanes can also use these techniques to block an active scan, although the mundane's ability to resist depends on how strong the telepath is.[13] Blocks can be broken by a sufficiently strong and/ or well trained teep, however doing so forcefully can lead to the subject suffering strokes, aneurysms or cerebral hemorrhaging.[11]
This can also refer to subconscious conditioning that restrains a subject at the point of action.[2][8]

Boot: Psi Corps security officers. Not full Psi Cops, they usually operated in support roles such as Bloodhound units.[2]

Bloodhound: Psi Corps tracking units, usually operating under the direction of a full Psi Cop.[2]

Busybody: Slang term for a commercial telepath.[2]

Cadre: Training groups composed of young telepaths, organized into boarding houses according to age group.[2]
Cadre Prime: A cadre of telepaths whose abilities manifested either at birth or before the onset of puberty. Housed separately from the other cadres, they account for less than 5% of all telepaths, and as such they are considered exceptionally rare and special. Other Cadres include Cadre Secundus and Cadre Tertius.[2]

Casting: (See "Mindcast")
Cops 'n' Blips: An approved game played by children in the Psi Corps during "constructive playtime". Generally it involves one or two children ("the blips") who are tasked with getting to a prearranged location without being caught, while the others (the "cops") attempt to track and capture them.[2]
Deathbed Scan: Performed when a telepath combs a dying person's mind for vital information up until the very moment of death. Such scans are known to be harmful to the telepath's mental health, with some believing that one loses a piece of one's soul by being in contact with the soon-to-decease person as they cross the threshold. Almost no telepath who has done such a scan willingly does one a second time, since subsequent attempts are thought to be very damaging to the psyche.[12] Psi Cop Alfred Bester repeatedly volunteered for such duty, once even following a subject's mind into the void. During that scan Bester very nearly died himself, and would have if not for the resuscitation efforts of hospital staff attending the dying subject. Some in the Corps say that Bester is the way he is because the better part of his soul is missing.[12]
Fugue: Telepathic attack. A favorite trick of blips, a fugue forces the target's mind to suddenly repeat its last thought over and over, effectively freezing the person's mind in the moment. The effect is short lived, but if timed right it can be enough to give the attacker an edge.[1] For a telepath, a fugue state is akin to a psi seizure or stroke, and can sometimes be brought on by extremely severe emotional distress or shock.[2]
Grabber, The: A children's nickname for William Karges and the statue that bore his likeness in Teeptown's alpha quad. Destroyed during the Telepath War, what was left was eventually removed and replaced by a statue of Matthew and Fiona Dexter with their lost baby Stephen in 2281.[14]
Grins: Term used by Psi Corps children for the faceless monitors within Psi Corps Cadre Prime youth training programs. Noted for their grey robes, almost mechanical voices, impersonal nature, and their blank featureless masks that display only very basic emotional symbols. Dealing out both punishments and rewards, they are more often than not a source of apprehension and mystery for most teep children. At age 12, the children are shown the true identities of the Grins, who are revealed to be their teachers and caregivers during a ceremony in which they receive their first pair of gloves.[2]

Glyph: Projection of a telepathic image. Can be used as a means of deception (making a subject think they saw something they didn't) or to accentuate communication through illustration.[2]
John Trakker, Psi Cop: Fictional character that features in a weekly vid series produced by the Psi Corps. A Psi Cop that works with his partner Heng, every week they work to capture "evil" and "stupid" rogue telepaths and send them off to be re-educated by the Corps. Also featured on a merchandising line based on the show.[2]
Latent: Referring to a telepath who has scored positive on the screening test, but whose ability has not yet manifested. Also called "late bloomers".[2][11][15]
Later: Referring to a telepath whose ability manifested after or during puberty.[2]
Mindblast: A sudden and powerful brute-force telepathic attack, a mindblast leaves its target in a telepathic fugue. Partial amnesia is also a common side effect of a mindblast.[2]
Mindburst: A sudden and debilitating burst of background "noise" from other minds, most commonly suffered by laters as their psi ability first manifests itself. The mindburst's intensity is directly proportional to the teep's psi rating. For example, to a P10 the experience is akin to a deaf person suddenly hearing a rocket engine right by their heads. The sudden shock can be severe enough as to render a teep unconscious.[16]
Mindcast: Direct telepathic communication.[2]
Mind shredder: Term applied to an individual trained in attack probes who has an exceptional knack for disrupting the abilities of other telepaths.[4]
Mindquake: A localized kinetic agitation, usually the result of an unstable teek who is unable to control their ability.[5]
Monitors: (See "Grins")
Mundane: non-telepath, meaning literally "normal". Often pejorative.[9]
P'see: Term used for a telepathic perception that manifests and is interpreted by a teep's brain as visual information, a sort of telepathic sight. Similar terms include "p'squint" and "p'hear".[2]
Psi Cop: Psi Corps police officers.
Rogue: (See "Blip")
Scan: An active telepathic probe. Surface scans, while difficult for even a trained P5 to detect, can only reveal what a person happens to be thinking from moment to moment and is routinely used in business negotiations to detect falsehoods, omission and obfuscation. A deep scan, while often uncomfortable, can uncover deeper thoughts and memories. Under certain conditions deep and extended scans can cause seizures, heart attacks, strokes, permanent brain damage, or if the subject is particularly resistant, death. Sustaining and blocking extended scans can also affect the telepath running the scan - the best human telepaths can only sustain a deep scan for up to 40–45 minutes, at which time they burst arteries, have strokes, or black out.[2][4][5][17]
Teep: Referring to any telepath.[15]
Teeptown: Closed community for telepaths in Geneva, originally built up by the MRA and later Psi Corps from the old "metasensory compound".[1][2]
Teek: Referring to any telekinetic. Noted for their tendency to "bloop".[15]
History
📷Psi Corps Headquarters
Early History
The beginnings of The Corps date back to 2117 and the formation of the Metasensory Regulation Authority (itself an outgrowth of the 2115 Senate Committee on Technology and Privacy and the subsequent Committee on Metasensory Regulation.) In 2156, following first contact with the Centauri Republic and the revelation that the Centauri and many other alien races possessed telepaths, it became apparent that Earth would need a more permanent and comprehensive solution than the MRA was able to provide. What finally tipped the balance of public opinion was the self-sacrifice of Earthforce Security Commander William Karges in thwarting of an assassination attempt on EA President Elizabeth Robinson in October of 2160. Karges had been an unregistered telepath and had used his ability to sense the thoughts of the bombers before they could detonate the President's motorcade. With this swing in public opinion concerning telepaths (which had until this point had been at its lowest since the pogroms of 2115), on April 12 2161, President Robinson was finally able to realize what Senator Lee Crawford had been working toward for decades and institute universal registration for Earth Alliance telepaths and an independently chartered MRA, dubbed "Psi Corps." Though the Karges incident is often credited by Psi Corps propaganda as the deciding factor, more cynical students of history have compared it to George Washington chopping down a cherry tree.[1][2][18] Robinson immediately offered Crawford the position of Director of the Psi Corps, though his tenure was short-lived, as on May 19, 2161, Crawford was assassinated while on his way to a meeting with Earth's first Centauri ambassador. Kevin Vacit, Crawford's assistant of nearly 30 years became the new Director.
While its public image was always that of a "friendly" service to society (though the facade was at times rather thin), under Vacit's direction, Psi Corps was fashioned into a keenly balanced machine, dedicated to honing and cultivating telepaths for the inevitable day when co-existence with mundanes would become a matter of survival. So adept was he at setting the Corps on its course that it could continue without him and without even knowing its true purpose.[1]
Collaboration with the Shadows and the underground railroad
Doctor Stephen Franklin participated in an underground railroad to help rogue telepaths escape from the Corps. Eventually, some of the telepaths who escaped provided assistance during the closing days of the Second Shadow war, while the highest levels of the Corps allied itself with the Shadows, providing them with captured rogue telepaths to operate on and surgically alter. Via Morden, the Shadows took an active role in the assassination of Luis Santiago, allowing some of their technology to be used by Earthforce.
After the Shadows and Vorlons left the galaxy with the other First Ones and Clark's defeat following the end of the Earth Alliance Civil War, a group of rogue telepaths led by Byron formed a small colony on Babylon 5, granted sanctuary by ISA President John Sheridan. The situation later ended in violence when the Psi Cops attempted to take the rogue telepaths back to Earth.
Telepath War
After the colony on Babylon 5 was forced to leave following the death of its leader, Byron, Lyta Alexander began a crusade against the Psi Corps. Her actions led to a conflict in which both rogue telepaths and mundanes fought against the Psi Corps. This conflict would later become known as the Telepath War.
Having lost the power it held during the Clark administration, the Psi Corps attempted to take over Earth's government, but eventually was defeated by the Earth Alliance, aided by the Interstellar Alliance and the rogue telepaths.
Aftermath
Following the end of the Telepath War, Psi Corps was formally dissolved, and the Earth Alliance began to take steps to re-integrate its telepaths into mainstream society. Freeing them from many of the past rules and restrictions, teeps were now allowed a much wider range of options as to what they chose to do with their lives, such as serving in Earthforce and working in the private sector. Many private schools were set up to educate telepaths around this time, though their success rate was somewhat mixed.
After the dissolution of Psi Corps, the Psionic Monitoring Commission was created, dedicated to hunting down those members of the Corps who had committed war crimes such as Alfred Bester. Eventually captured and put on trial for his past atrocities, Bester was sentenced to spend the rest of his life in prison, his abilities taken away by the very sleepers that he once administered to countless blips.
Some Psi Corps members, like John Matheson, joined later Earthforce.

📰 Article:

I genuinely cannot believe I'm writing this about the sitting Premier of Manitoba, and not because Wab Kinew criticized Donald Trump, wants the Epstein files released, or thinks Trump's foreign policy is a flaming catastrophe. Fill your boots. None of that is particularly remarkable.

I'm writing this because I've now watched the Premier of Manitoba repeatedly take his own suspicions about Trump, Epstein and the Iran war and present them publicly with increasing certainty, without producing the evidence that would justify that certainty. Somewhere between “this might explain it” and “this is why it happened,” speculation quietly became fact simply because Wab Kinew started speaking as though it were.

It isn't.

In early March of this year, while discussing the “why” of the war with Iran with reporters, Kinew offered the Epstein files as “as good of a reason as anyone else can figure out.”

Stop right there, because that is speculation. It's a theory. A guess. Something Kinew apparently believed might explain what was happening. Premiers are allowed to speculate, although one might reasonably expect the head of a provincial government to make it abundantly clear when he's doing so. Maybe he's right. Maybe he isn't. Unless somebody from MI6 rappelled through the Premier's window overnight and left a dossier marked FOR WAB'S EYES ONLY, the rest of us still require evidence.

But then, on March 24, something remarkable had happened. Kinew declared, “They started this war as a distraction from the Epstein files.”

Oh. They did?

Apparently the dossier arrived. Somewhere between maybe and definitely, our Premier appears to have been promoted to 00-Wab. Licence to Speculate.

So what happened in between? What new evidence emerged? What intelligence briefing established the motive? Which documents proved it? Who confirmed it? Because we're no longer talking about a premier tossing out a theory. We're talking about the Premier of Manitoba publicly accusing the President of the United States of starting a war to conceal or distract from the Epstein files.

That is an extraordinary accusation against any president. Making it against Donald Trump, of all presidents, adds another layer of bewilderment. Whatever anyone thinks of Trump, his tendency to respond aggressively to personal attacks is hardly classified information. The man has turned taking things personally into something resembling foreign policy.

Canadian governments are simultaneously trying to manage an already difficult relationship with the United States, our largest trading partner, while provincial premiers including David Eby, Kinew and Doug Ford seem remarkably comfortable supplying fresh reasons for that relationship to become even more antagonistic.

This isn't an argument that Canadian politicians should be frightened of Donald Trump or refrain from criticizing him. Criticize his tariffs. Criticize his foreign policy. Criticize his decisions until the microphones wear out. But accusing him of deliberately starting a war to distract from Jeffrey Epstein is something else entirely.

If Kinew has evidence establishing that, produce it. If he doesn't, what in God's name is the Premier of Manitoba doing stating it publicly as fact In the arena of public opinion?

Because somewhere along the way Kinew simply vaulted over the rather important evidentiary chasm between “I suspect” and “I know,” apparently without noticing there was supposed to be a bridge. I find that genuinely astonishing.

When the Premier of Manitoba makes an accusation this serious in front of reporters, Canadians should not have to wonder whether we're hearing information supported by evidence or Wab Kinew's personal hunch with the authority of the Premier's Office stapled to it.

Three days later came the federal NDP convention. Kinew told the crowd: “No American child from the blue collar or the middle class should have to die in Iran. Let the Epstein class fight the Epstein war.”

And they gave him a standing ovation.

The line landed to raucous applause, with people actually getting to their feet to cheer. Evidence, apparently, was no longer required. 00-Wab had briefed the room.

Christ, even M made Bond bring back the bloody photographs.

Because apparently Canada's political culture has deteriorated to the point where nobody in that cheering room thought to ask the terribly unfashionable question: Is any of this actually proven?

Instead, clap clap clap, honk honk, blah blah Epstein, and off we go.

Then Epstein somehow wandered into Manitoba's liquor policy. During an April interview about what it would take to put American alcohol back on Manitoba shelves, Kinew suggested upping the ante by demanding release of the Epstein files before removing the booze ban.

Excuse me, but how in the hell did we get here?

At this point I can only assume Q Branch had quietly taken over the Premier’s Office. Somewhere beneath the Legislature, a nervous civil servant was presumably handing 00-Wab an exploding briefcase marked EPSTEIN: TOP SECRET, while Q demonstrated a fountain pen capable of detecting inconvenient gaps in evidence and warned him, “Careful, Premier. That detects missing evidence. It doesn’t magically create it.”

I realize that sounds ridiculous. That's rather the point. Because spontaneously slipping up once or twice, fine. Politicians make provocative comments. They troll, and they exaggerate. They say something stupid because somebody put a television camera within fifty feet of them. But Kinew… Kinew keeps doing it.

It's always the same pattern with this man, and every time he returns to the subject, he sounds a little more certain than he did the last time. What began as maybe this explains it somehow became this is what happened, without that annoying little part in the middle where somebody is supposed to produce undeniable evidence.

A suspicion became a theory. The theory became a claim. The claim became a slogan. And eventually, the slogan became something he apparently felt perfectly comfortable repeating as factual, gospel truth.

And now, on September 9, we get this: “Release the Epstein files. Donald Trump is Jeffrey Epstein's best friend. The reason why we're at war in Iran and everyone's paying higher gas prices is because of the Epstein files.”

Sweet merciful Christ. 00-Wab has cracked the whole operation. Epstein. Trump. Iran. The war. Gas prices. It’s all right there.

Apparently somewhere between Winnipeg and Tehran, Manitoba’s Premier parachuted from a burning helicopter, skied down a mountain in a tuxedo, seduced a double agent, recovered the microfilm, escaped an exploding submarine and returned to the Legislature before Question Period carrying intelligence unavailable to the rest of Western civilization.

And apparently the only thing he forgot to bring back was the f*cking evidence.

Now back here on boring old Planet Earth, there are established facts. Trump knew Jeffrey Epstein socially. Their past association is documented. Epstein was a convicted sex offender whose crimes and relationships with powerful people unquestionably deserve investigation.

Fine. Investigate everything. Release everything legally releasable. Prosecute anybody against whom admissible evidence establishes a crime. That's how a functioning society is supposed to work.

But “Trump knew Epstein” and “Trump started a war to distract everyone from Epstein” are not the same statement.

There is an enormous evidentiary canyon between them. You don't get to bridge it with suspicion, repetition and a sufficiently confident tone of voice. And you certainly don't get to declare yourself safely on the other side simply because nobody stopped you.

And what should bother every Manitoban most: if this is how Kinew gets from “I think” to “I know” when he's talking about Donald Trump, what happens when the subject is something he actually has the power to decide? If Wab Kinew is this comfortable publicly converting inference into certainty, what standard does he apply when somebody walks into the Premier's Office with an allegation? What does he require before accepting advice? Before judging somebody's motives? Before making policy? Before spending public money? Before making decisions affecting businesses, families or communities?

Those aren't rhetorical cheap shots. They're questions about judgment.

A premier should have unusually good judgment. He should be difficult to fool. He should be skeptical. He should demand evidence. He should understand the difference between possible, plausible, probable and proven without needing somebody from the Justice Department to draw him a freaking diagram.

Maybe somewhere beneath the Manitoba Legislature there really is a subterranean command centre with a giant map of Iran, a shark tank and an unnecessarily complicated conference table that slowly rotates into the floor. If so, somebody please take me downstairs. I have questions for M. Otherwise we're left with the considerably less entertaining possibility that Kinew simply believes this.

And then there's the applause. I'm not sure which troubles me more: that Kinew keeps saying this stuff, or that thousands of Canadians hear it and respond like seals waiting for somebody to throw another Epstein-shaped herring onto the stage.

Wake up. We've got massive problems in this country.

You can despise Donald Trump and still demand evidence. You can believe every Epstein document should be released and still demand evidence. You can oppose the Iran war and still demand evidence. Those positions are not contradictory. They're what intellectual adulthood looks like.

And Manitoba voters should seriously consider what they're watching. Is this what you elected? Did you elect a premier to govern Manitoba, or did Manitoba accidentally elect 00-Wab, Her Majesty's Secret Premier, licensed to roam the international stage solving geopolitical mysteries before returning to Winnipeg in time for Cabinet?
Because at some point this stops being funny.

His office matters. His words travel outside Manitoba and outside Canada. Foreigners hearing a Canadian premier confidently announce unproven motives for an American war aren't necessarily thinking, What a courageous truth-teller. Some of them are probably wondering what the hell happened to us. And frankly, so am I.

Wab Kinew can hate Trump. He can demand the files. He can condemn the war. He can campaign against American tariffs. But he needs to stop using the authority of the Premier's Office to elevate whatever he personally believes into established fact.

Maybe I'm being unfair. Maybe somewhere behind Kinew's desk there's a bookcase that swings open at midnight, revealing a steel staircase descending beneath the Manitoba Legislature.

Maybe down there is a windowless situation room where M waits beside a glowing map while Q wheels out a tricked-out snowmobile with machine guns behind the headlights and a licence plate that rotates between FRIENDLY MANITOBA and FOR WAB'S EYES ONLY. Maybe a beautiful double agent arrives from Tehran carrying the missing documents in a briefcase handcuffed to her wrist.

Maybe Kinew receives his instructions, straightens his tuxedo, downs a martini, walks through the secret tunnel beneath Broadway and emerges beside the Golden Boy just as the Manitoba Legislature explodes behind him for absolutely no defensible reason.

If that's happening, I owe the man an apology. If it isn't, we're back to asking where the hell his evidence is.

Because leadership requires something considerably more difficult than certainty. It requires knowing when you don't know.

If Wab Kinew possesses evidence establishing that Donald Trump started a war to distract from the Epstein files, then by all means, produce the damn thing. Surely after all this international espionage, 00-Wab can emerge from the vault with something more substantial than his own certainty. Have Q retrieve the microfilm, get M on the secure line, drag the Aston Martin around front and tell Moneypenny lunch is cancelled. Hell, if somebody absolutely has to escape an exploding submarine or send a henchman skiing magnificently off a cliff before Manitobans are finally permitted to see the evidence, apparently that's where we are now.

Just produce the evidence, Premier. 

Because until you do, you're not James Bond. You're the Premier of Manitoba standing in front of television cameras telling Canadians that your personal theory about the President of the United States is established fact. And no amount of confidence changes that.

Wab Kinew may have given himself a Licence to Speculate, but Manitobans gave him a licence to govern. Perhaps it's time he remembered which one is real.
